q: The SI unit of work is the joule. One joule is equal to:
x: Work = force × displacement, so 1 J = 1 N × 1 m = 1 N m. The newton-second is the unit of impulse, and kg m s⁻¹ is the unit of momentum.

q: Energy of a body is defined as its:
x: A body has energy if it is able to do work. The rate of doing work is power.

q: The law of conservation of energy states that:
o: Energy is always converted completely into useful work
The kinetic energy of a system always remains constant
Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only changed from one form to another
Energy can be created when work is done on a body
x: In an isolated system the total energy stays constant; energy only changes form. Kinetic energy alone need not stay constant.

q: For absolute gravitational potential energy, the zero of potential energy is taken at:
x: Absolute PE is measured from a point infinitely far from the Earth, where the gravitational force and the PE are both zero.

q: A force of 20 N acts on a body at 60° to its displacement of 5 m. The work done by the force is (cos 60° = 0.5):
x: W = Fd cos θ = 20 × 5 × 0.5 = 50 J. Using sin 60° instead of cos 60° gives the wrong value 50√3 J.

q: One kilowatt-hour (kWh) is equal to:
x: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. Forgetting to change hours into seconds or kilowatts into watts gives the smaller values.

q: A ball falls freely from a height with no air resistance. As it falls:
o: Its potential and kinetic energies both decrease
Its potential energy increases and its kinetic energy decreases
Its potential energy decreases, its kinetic energy increases, and the total stays constant
x: Without air resistance, the loss of gravitational potential energy equals the gain of kinetic energy, so the total mechanical energy is constant.

q: The absolute gravitational potential energy of a body near the Earth is negative because:
o: The body is always moving towards the Earth
The force is attractive, so work must be done on the body to take it to infinity where PE is zero
The mass of the body is taken as negative
Gravitational potential energy is a vector pointing downward
x: Since gravity attracts, energy must be supplied to move the body out to infinity, where U = 0. So at any finite distance its PE is less than zero.

q: A stone tied to a string is whirled in a horizontal circle at constant speed. The work done by the tension (centripetal force) in one revolution is:
o: Equal to the kinetic energy of the stone
Negative and equal to the kinetic energy
x: The centripetal force always acts towards the centre, at 90° to the displacement at every instant, and cos 90° = 0, so it does no work.

q: Which of the following is NOT a unit of energy?
x: The watt (J s⁻¹) is a unit of power. The joule, kilowatt-hour and electron volt all measure energy.

q: In a hydroelectric power station, the energy changes in the correct order are:
o: Kinetic energy of water → potential energy of water → electrical energy
Potential energy of stored water → kinetic energy of water → electrical energy
Chemical energy → heat energy → electrical energy
Electrical energy → kinetic energy → potential energy
x: Water stored at a height has gravitational potential energy; it falls and gains kinetic energy, which turns the turbines and the generator to give electrical energy.

q: As a satellite moves farther from the Earth, its absolute gravitational potential energy:
o: Increases and becomes large and positive
Increases, becoming less negative and approaching zero
x: U = −GMm/r. As r increases, U gets closer to zero from below, so it increases, but it never becomes positive.

q: A man carries a 10 kg bag on his head and walks 20 m along a level road at constant velocity. The work done by the upward force he exerts on the bag is:
x: The upward force is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement (θ = 90°), so W = Fd cos 90° = 0, even though he may feel tired.

q: A 2 kg ball is dropped from a height of 20 m. Ignoring air resistance, its kinetic energy when it is 5 m above the ground is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: KE gained = loss in PE = mg(20 − 5) = 2 × 10 × 15 = 300 J. Using h = 5 m gives 100 J, and the total energy is 400 J.

q: A body is taken from point X to a higher point Y, once along a straight path and once along a winding path. The work done against gravity is:
x: Gravity is a conservative force: the work done against it depends only on the starting and finishing heights, not on the path taken.

q: The absolute gravitational potential energy of a mass m on the surface of the Earth (mass M, radius R) is:
x: Absolute PE = −GMm/r with r = R at the surface. −GMm/R² is the form of the force, and −GM/R has no mass of the body, so it is not an energy.

q: Work is a scalar quantity because it is:
o: The scalar (dot) product of force and displacement
The vector (cross) product of force and displacement
The product of force and time
The ratio of force to displacement
x: W = F · d = Fd cos θ. The dot product of two vectors gives a scalar; the cross product would give a vector.

q: A body at rest on a smooth (frictionless) horizontal surface has 50 J of work done on it by a horizontal force. The body:
o: Gains no energy, because the surface is horizontal
x: With no friction and no change in height, all the work done on the body appears as kinetic energy (work–energy principle).

q: A body is moved around a closed path in Earth's gravitational field and returns to its starting point. The total work done by gravity is:
o: Equal to mgh for the highest point
Equal to the weight times the path length
x: Gravity is conservative, so the work done by it around any closed path is zero; the body returns to the same height with the same gravitational PE.

q: A 5 kg mass is lifted vertically upward through 2 m at constant speed. The work done by the lifting force is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: At constant speed the lifting force equals the weight, mg = 5 × 10 = 50 N. W = 50 × 2 = 100 J. Forgetting g gives 10 J.

q: Which statement about energy is correct?
o: It is a vector quantity with the same unit as work
It is a scalar quantity with the same unit as power
It is a scalar quantity with the same unit as work
It is a vector quantity with the same unit as momentum
x: Energy has magnitude only, so it is a scalar, and it is measured in joules like work, since energy is the capacity to do work.

q: Power is defined as:
o: The product of force and time
The work done per unit displacement
x: P = W/t, the work done per unit time. The ability to do work is energy, and work per unit displacement is force.

q: A spring is stretched slowly from its natural length by 0.5 m. The force needed rises uniformly from 0 N to 40 N. The work done in stretching it is:
x: Work is the area under the force–displacement graph, a triangle: W = ½ × 40 × 0.5 = 10 J. Forgetting the ½ (treating the force as 40 N throughout) gives 20 J.

q: A force of 20 N pushes a body along a straight line for the first 2 m. Over the next 3 m the force falls uniformly from 20 N to zero. The total work done by the force over the 5 m is:
x: Area under the F–x graph: rectangle 20 × 2 = 40 J plus triangle ½ × 20 × 3 = 30 J, total 70 J. Taking 20 N over the whole 5 m gives 100 J; counting only one part gives 40 J or 30 J.

q: A 4 kg block is pushed 5 m along a horizontal floor. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25 (g = 10 m s⁻²). The magnitude of the work done by friction on the block is:
x: Friction f = μmg = 0.25 × 4 × 10 = 10 N, so its work has magnitude f d = 10 × 5 = 50 J. Leaving out μ gives mgd = 200 J; 10 J is only the force, not the work.

q: A 2 kg block slides 10 m down the full length of a smooth incline that makes 30° with the horizontal. The work done by gravity on the block is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: The vertical drop is 10 sin 30° = 5 m, so W = mgh = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J (same as mg sin 30° × 10). Using cos 30° instead of sin 30° gives 100√3 J; ignoring the angle gives 200 J.

q: A constant force F = (3i + 4j) N acts on a particle while it moves through a displacement d = (2i − j) m. The work done by the force is:
x: W = F·d = (3)(2) + (4)(−1) = 6 − 4 = 2 J. Ignoring the minus sign of the j component gives 6 + 4 = 10 J.

q: For a variable force acting along a straight line, the area under the force–displacement graph gives the:
o: Change in momentum of the body
x: Each strip of the F–x graph has area F Δx, which is the work done over Δx; adding the strips gives the total work. Impulse and change of momentum are the area under a force–time graph, the most common mix-up.

q: A 0.5 kg ball moves at 4 m s⁻¹. Its kinetic energy is:
x: K = ½mv² = ½ × 0.5 × 16 = 4 J. Forgetting the ½ gives 8 J; forgetting to square v gives ½ × 0.5 × 4 = 1 J.

q: The linear momentum of a body of fixed mass is doubled. Its kinetic energy becomes:
x: K = p²/2m, so with m fixed K ∝ p²; doubling p makes K four times as large. Taking K proportional to p gives the tempting answer of twice.

q: Two bodies of masses 1 kg and 4 kg have equal kinetic energies. The ratio of their momenta (1 kg body : 4 kg body) is:
x: p = √(2mK); with K equal, p ∝ √m, so p₁ : p₂ = √1 : √4 = 1 : 2. Forgetting the square root gives 1 : 4.

q: A 2 kg block moving at 10 m s⁻¹ slides onto a rough horizontal surface that exerts a constant friction force of 5 N on it. How far does it slide before stopping?
x: By the work–energy principle, f d = ½mv²: 5 d = ½ × 2 × 100 = 100 J, so d = 20 m. Forgetting the ½ in the kinetic energy gives 40 m.

q: A 20 g bullet moving at 300 m s⁻¹ hits a fixed wooden block and stops after penetrating 10 cm. The average resistive force of the wood on the bullet is:
x: K = ½ × 0.02 × 300² = 900 J; F = K/d = 900/0.1 = 9 × 10³ N. Forgetting the ½ gives 1.8 × 10⁴ N; using 10 m for 10 cm gives 90 N; using 20 kg for 20 g gives 9 × 10⁶ N.

q: The escape velocity from the surface of a planet of mass M and radius R is:
x: Setting ½mv² = GMm/R gives v_esc = √(2GM/R). √(GM/R) is the orbital speed close to the surface, the usual confusion.

q: Taking g = 10 m s⁻² at the Earth's surface and the Earth's radius as 6.4 × 10⁶ m, the escape velocity from the Earth is:
x: v_esc = √(2gR) = √(2 × 10 × 6.4 × 10⁶) = √(1.28 × 10⁸) = 8√2 × 10³ m s⁻¹ ≈ 11.3 km s⁻¹. Leaving out the 2 gives √(gR) = 8 km s⁻¹, the orbital speed near the surface.

q: A planet has the same radius as the Earth but four times its mass. If the escape velocity from the Earth is v, the escape velocity from this planet is:
x: v_esc = √(2GM/R) ∝ √M at fixed R, so 4 times the mass gives √4 = 2 times the escape velocity, 2v. Forgetting the square root gives 4v.

q: A planet has 8 times the mass and 2 times the radius of the Earth. If the escape velocity from the Earth is v, the escape velocity from the planet is:
x: v_esc ∝ √(M/R) = √(8/2) = √4 = 2, so it is 2v. Forgetting the square root gives 4v; ignoring the radius change gives √8 v, and ignoring the root and radius gives 8v.

q: Ignoring air resistance and the Earth's rotation, the minimum energy needed to take a 100 kg body from the Earth's surface to infinity is (g = 10 m s⁻², Earth's radius 6.4 × 10⁶ m):
x: The absolute PE at the surface is −GMm/R, so the work needed is GMm/R = mgR (since GM = gR²) = 100 × 10 × 6.4 × 10⁶ = 6.4 × 10⁹ J. Leaving out g gives 6.4 × 10⁸ J; halving or doubling mgR gives the other values.

q: A 2 kg body needs a launch speed of 11.2 km s⁻¹ to escape from the Earth. The launch speed a 4 kg body needs to escape from the Earth is:
x: In ½mv² = GMm/R the mass m cancels, so v_esc = √(2GM/R) does not depend on the body's mass: still 11.2 km s⁻¹. The other values come from wrongly scaling with m or √m.

q: A body of mass m is raised from the Earth's surface to a height equal to the Earth's radius R. With g the acceleration due to gravity at the surface, the increase in its gravitational potential energy is:
x: ΔU = −GMm/2R − (−GMm/R) = GMm/2R = ½mgR, using GM = gR². Using mgh with h = R gives mgR, which wrongly assumes g stays constant up to that height.

q: An electric hoist lifts a 50 kg load vertically through 12 m at constant speed in 20 s. The useful power it delivers is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: P = mgh/t = 50 × 10 × 12 / 20 = 300 W. Leaving out g gives 30 W; giving the work 6000 J instead of dividing by time gives 6000 W.

q: A car moves at a constant 20 m s⁻¹ on a level road against a total resistive force of 1500 N. The power developed by its engine is:
x: At constant speed the driving force equals the resistance, so P = Fv = 1500 × 20 = 30 000 W = 30 kW. A power-of-ten slip gives 3 kW or 300 kW; taking half of Fv gives 15 kW.

q: A pump raises 600 kg of water every minute through a height of 10 m. Its efficiency is 50 %. The input power of the pump is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: Useful power = mgh/t = 600 × 10 × 10 / 60 = 1000 W; input = useful ÷ efficiency = 1000 / 0.5 = 2000 W = 2 kW. Stopping at the useful power gives 1 kW; multiplying by 0.5 gives 0.5 kW; dividing by 1 s instead of 60 s gives 120 kW.

q: Which of these forces is non-conservative?
x: The work done by friction depends on the path taken and is turned into heat, so friction is non-conservative. Gravitational, elastic and electrostatic forces do path-independent work and are conservative.

q: A 2 kg body starts from rest and slides down a rough curved track, losing 5 m in height. It reaches the bottom at 8 m s⁻¹. The work done against friction is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: Loss of PE = mgh = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J; gain of KE = ½ × 2 × 64 = 64 J; the difference, 100 − 64 = 36 J, is the work done against friction. 64 J is only the KE gained.
